topics.title: SQL basics
topics.subtitle: Foundational SQL every DE must know cold

questions.question: What is the order SQL clauses execute?
questions.hint: Not the order you write them

answer.html:
SQL processes in this order: FROM → JOIN → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY → LIMIT.

This is why you cannot use a SELECT alias inside WHERE — WHERE runs before SELECT.

questions.question: WHERE vs HAVING — what is the difference?

answer.html:
WHERE filters rows before grouping. Cannot use aggregates.
HAVING filters after grouping. Must use aggregates.

answer.code:
-- WHERE: filter raw rows
WHERE customer_state = 'SP'

-- HAVING: filter aggregated groups
GROUP BY customer_state
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1000

questions.question: What is GROUP BY and when do you use it?

answer.html: GROUP BY collapses multiple rows into one row per unique value. Use it when you want totals, counts, or averages by a category.

answer.code:
SELECT order_status, COUNT(*) AS total
FROM olist_orders
GROUP BY order_status
ORDER BY total DESC;

questions.question: What is DISTINCT and when should you avoid it?

answer.html: DISTINCT removes duplicate rows. Avoid it when duplicates come from a bad JOIN — fix the join instead. It is also expensive on large tables.

answer.code:
SELECT DISTINCT payment_type FROM olist_order_payments;
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT customer_unique_id) FROM olist_customers;

questions.question: How do you handle NULLs in SQL?

answer.html: NULL means unknown. Never use = NULL — always use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL. Use COALESCE to replace nulls. Use NULLIF to prevent divide-by-zero.

answer.code:
WHERE order_approved_at IS NULL
COALESCE(comment, 'No comment')
NULLIF(total_orders, 0)

questions.question: What are the JOIN types and when to use each?

rows: You only want rows matched in both tables
All left rows even if no match
You want everything regardless of match

answer.html: Find rows in left table with NO match in right. Write it as LEFT JOIN + WHERE right.key IS NULL.

answer.code:
-- Orders with no review
SELECT o.order_id
FROM olist_orders o
LEFT JOIN olist_order_reviews r ON o.order_id = r.order_id
WHERE r.order_id IS NULL;

answer.html: A self join joins a table to itself. Use when you want to compare rows within the same table.

answer.code:
SELECT s1.seller_id, s2.seller_id, s1.seller_city
FROM olist_sellers s1
JOIN olist_sellers s2
  ON s1.seller_city = s2.seller_city
  AND s1.seller_id < s2.seller_id;

topics.title: Window functions
topics.subtitle: The hardest SQL topic in every senior DE interview

sections.title: OVER, PARTITION BY, ORDER BY explained

answer.html: A window function performs a calculation across rows related to the current row — without collapsing rows like GROUP BY does. You keep all rows AND get the calculated value on each row.
PARTITION BY divides rows into groups and restarts the window calculation for each group. Think of it as "do this calculation separately per group".

answer.code:
-- Ranks across ALL sellers
RANK() OVER (ORDER BY revenue DESC)

-- Ranks within each state separately
RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY seller_state ORDER BY revenue DESC)

questions.question: What does ORDER BY do inside OVER?

answer.html: ORDER BY inside OVER defines the sequence within the window. Required for RANK, ROW_NUMBER, LAG, LEAD, and running totals. Completely separate from the ORDER BY at the end that sorts final results.

questions.question: How do you remove duplicates using ROW_NUMBER?

answer.html: LAG looks at the previous row. LEAD looks at the next row.

answer.code:
-- MoM change
total - LAG(total) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS change

-- Next order date per customer
LEAD(order_date) OVER (
  PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date
) AS next_order

-- Running total
SUM(payment_value) OVER (
  PARTITION BY payment_type ORDER BY order_id
) AS running_total

-- 7-day moving average
AVG(total_orders) OVER (
  ORDER BY order_date
  ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
) AS avg_7d

questions.question: How do you find duplicate rows?

SELECT customer_unique_id, COUNT(*) AS cnt
FROM olist_customers

HAVING COUNT(*) > 1

questions.question: How do you remove duplicates and keep the latest?

answer.html: Only pull records newer than the last successful run watermark.

questions.question: Pivot rows into columns with CASE WHEN

answer.code:
SELECT customer_state,
  COUNT(CASE WHEN order_status='delivered' THEN 1 END) delivered,
  COUNT(CASE WHEN order_status='canceled'  THEN 1 END) canceled,
  COUNT(CASE WHEN order_status='shipped'   THEN 1 END) shipped
FROM olist_orders o
JOIN olist_customers c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
GROUP BY customer_state;

-- Replace NULL with default
COALESCE(review_comment_message, 'No comment')

-- Prevent divide by zero
revenue / NULLIF(total_orders, 0)

-- Multiple fallbacks
COALESCE(preferred_name, first_name, 'Unknown')

WITH stats AS (
  SELECT
    AVG(DATEDIFF(day, order_purchase_timestamp,
      order_delivered_customer_date)) AS avg_days,
    STDDEV(DATEDIFF(day, order_purchase_timestamp,
      order_delivered_customer_date)) AS sd
  FROM olist_orders
  WHERE order_delivered_customer_date IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT o.order_id,
  DATEDIFF(day, order_purchase_timestamp,
    order_delivered_customer_date) AS delivery_days
FROM olist_orders o, stats s
WHERE DATEDIFF(day, order_purchase_timestamp,
  order_delivered_customer_date) > s.avg_days + 2*s.sd;

topics.title: How to read and write a SQL query
topics.subtitle: The 5-step framework to go from question to answer

questions.question: Step 1 — Read the question in plain English

answer.html:
Before writing SQL, ask: What do I want to see in the result?

Example: "Find top 10 states by number of customers"
→ I want a list of states with a count, sorted highest to lowest, top 10 only.

answer.code:
customers   → olist_customers
orders      → olist_orders
payments    → olist_order_payments
reviews     → olist_order_reviews
products    → olist_products
sellers     → olist_sellers

answer.html:
Ask: What columns do I want back?

For "top 10 states by customers" → customer_state and COUNT(*)

questions.question: Step 4 — Add clauses in execution order

answer.code:
SELECT    -- what columns?
FROM      -- which table?
JOIN      -- need another table?
WHERE     -- row-level filters?
GROUP BY  -- aggregating?
HAVING    -- filter after grouping?
ORDER BY  -- how to sort?
LIMIT     -- top N only?

questions.question: Step 5 — Read it back in plain English

answer.html: "Give me customer_state and count, from olist_customers, grouped by state, ordered descending, top 10 only"

answer.code:
SELECT customer_state, COUNT(*) AS total
FROM RAW.PUBLIC.olist_customers
GROUP BY customer_state
ORDER BY total DESC
LIMIT 10;

topics.title: DE concepts

answer.html: A series of automated steps that move and transform data from a source to a destination. Typically includes ingestion, validation, transformation, and loading into a warehouse.

questions.question: What is idempotency and why does it matter?

answer.html: An idempotent pipeline produces the same result no matter how many times you run it with the same input. Critical because pipelines fail and get rerun. Use MERGE/upsert or deduplicate after load to ensure idempotency.

questions.question: What is CDC — Change Data Capture?

answer.html: CDC tracks changes (inserts, updates, deletes) in a source database and replicates them to your warehouse in near real-time. Tools: Debezium, AWS DMS, Fivetran. Most common method: log-based CDC using the database transaction log.

questions.question: What is a slowly changing dimension (SCD)?

rows: New row per change — full history with effective dates
Extra column for previous value — one historical version

topics.title: Data modeling
topics.subtitle: How to design data structures that work in production

answer.html: A design technique for data warehouses that organizes data into fact tables (measurable events) and dimension tables (context/descriptors). Optimized for query performance and analyst readability. Developed by Ralph Kimball.

questions.question: What is grain in data modeling?

answer.html: Grain defines what a single row in a fact table represents. You must define grain before adding any columns. Example: "one row per order item" vs "one row per order" vs "one row per customer per day". Getting grain wrong means all your aggregations will be wrong.

questions.question: What is Apache Spark and why use it?

answer.html: Spark is a distributed computing framework that processes large datasets across a cluster. Use it when data is too large for a single machine (typically >10GB). Processes data in-memory making it 100x faster than Hadoop MapReduce for most workloads.

answer.code:
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, functions as F

spark = SparkSession.builder.appName("Stackle").getOrCreate()
df = spark.read.csv("olist_orders.csv", header=True, inferSchema=True)

df.filter(F.col("order_status") == "delivered") \
  .groupBy("customer_state") \
  .agg(F.count("*").alias("total")) \
  .orderBy("total", ascending=False) \
  .show(10)

topics.title: Snowflake
topics.subtitle: Cloud data warehouse architecture and key features

answer.html: Snowflake separates storage and compute. Storage lives in cloud object storage (S3/Azure Blob). Compute runs on virtual warehouses that scale instantly and pause when idle. Multiple warehouses can query the same data simultaneously without contention.

questions.question: QUALIFY — filter on window fn result

answer.code:
SELECT seller_id, seller_state, SUM(price) revenue,
  RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY seller_state ORDER BY SUM(price) DESC) rnk
FROM olist_order_items oi
JOIN olist_sellers s USING (seller_id)
GROUP BY 1,2
QUALIFY rnk = 1;

questions.question: What is dbt and what problem does it solve?

answer.html: dbt lets you write SELECT statements and handles creating tables/views, running them in order, testing them, and documenting them. It brings software engineering practices (version control, testing, CI/CD) to SQL transformation.
A .sql file containing a SELECT statement. dbt compiles it and creates a table or view in your warehouse. Use ref() to reference other models — dbt builds the dependency graph automatically.

Kafka is a distributed event streaming platform. Producers write events to topics. Consumers read from topics at their own pace. Kafka retains events for a configurable period so consumers can replay data.

questions.question: What is a DAG in Airflow?

answer.html: A DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph) is a collection of tasks with defined dependencies. "Directed" = tasks flow one direction. "Acyclic" = no circular dependencies. Each DAG has a schedule and a start date.

answer.code:
with DAG('olist_pipeline',
         start_date=datetime(2024,1,1),
         schedule_interval='@daily') as dag:
    extract >> transform >> load

questions.question: How is AI changing data engineering?

answer.html:
DEs now embed LLMs directly into pipelines to:

1. Generate and optimize SQL
2. Classify and tag data automatically
3. Extract entities from unstructured text
4. Generate data quality rules
5. Monitor pipelines with natural language alerts
6. Build RAG pipelines on structured data

questions.question: Call the Claude API inside a Python pipeline

answer.code:
import anthropic, pandas as pd

client = anthropic.Anthropic(api_key="YOUR_KEY")

def classify_review(text: str) -> str:
    msg = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-sonnet-4-20250514",
        max_tokens=100,
        messages=[{"role":"user",
          "content":f"Classify as positive/negative/neutral: {text}"}]
    )
    return msg.content[0].text

df['sentiment'] = df['review_comment_message'].apply(classify_review)

questions.question: What is RAG and how does it apply to DE?

answer.html:
RAG (Retrieval Augmented Generation) combines vector search with an LLM. You retrieve relevant records from a vector store and pass them as context to the model.

DE use cases: natural language queries on your warehouse, intelligent data catalog search, automated data documentation.

topics.title: Behavioral + interview prep
topics.subtitle: How to answer the questions that decide the offer

answer.html:
Structure: Past → Present → Future

"I have X years in data engineering working with [technologies]. Most recently I have been building [specific work]. I want to join [type of company] where I can [specific goal]."

Keep it under 90 seconds. End with why you want THIS role.

questions.question: Tell me about a pipeline you built end to end

answer.html:
Use STAR: Situation → Task → Action → Result

Cover: source, destination, tools, challenges, business impact. Always end with a number — "reduced report latency from 4 hours to 15 minutes".

questions.question: How do you handle a pipeline that keeps failing?

answer.html:
1. Check logs — find the exact failing line
2. Reproduce locally
3. Determine: data issue or code issue
4. Add monitoring if missing
5. Fix root cause, not the symptom
6. Add a test to prevent recurrence
7. Document what happened

questions.question: Where is DE going in the next 3 years?

answer.html: Three things: AI integration (LLMs in pipelines, natural language interfaces), real-time everywhere (streaming replacing batch as tooling matures), and less plumbing more value (managed services handle infra, DEs focus on modeling, quality, and enabling the business).
